name: Viviscal

lead: Viviscal is a marine-protein supplement taken twice daily by men and women with thinning hair who want more density and thickness. Small placebo-controlled trials in women and in men with male pattern hair loss report more terminal hairs and less shedding.

Its marine complex is proposed to support the hair growth cycle, though human mechanistic evidence is limited. A 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review listed it among supplements with the highest-quality evidence of potential benefit, with a general caution about the field.

paras: It is taken as an oral supplement twice daily, with Extra Strength and Man versions. Trials were small and short, and users generally expect months of consistent use.
Trials report few or no adverse events, and a systematic review described supplement adverse effects as rare and mild. It is sold as a dietary supplement.

angle.text: Viviscal is taken by men and women with thinning hair who want more density and thickness. A marine protein complex is said to support follicle nutrition and the hair growth cycle. A few placebo-controlled trials report more terminal hairs, and a 2023 review is cautiously positive.

lead: Viviscal is a branded oral supplement built around a proprietary marine collagen complex, marketed for thinning hair in women and men. Its range includes Extra Strength, Professional Strength and Man versions, plus newer products for the hair growth cycle and for shedding; the formulas combine the marine complex with nutrients such as biotin, vitamin C, iron, zinc and copper.[1][2][3][2] People take it as a daily tablet or capsule in the hope of more terminal hairs, less shedding and a fuller look to thinning areas over several months.

Published placebo-controlled trials of Viviscal products, in women and in men with male pattern hair loss, report more terminal hairs and less shedding than placebo.[2][3] A 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review counted Viviscal among the supplements with the highest-quality evidence of potential benefit in people without a known deficiency, while advising cautious interpretation, and a 2026 meta-analysis of commercial oral supplements for hair growth listed it among the products assessed.[4][5]

The company says the brand's origin lies in a Scandinavian observation that marine proteins in the Inuit diet supported strong hair, that it has focused on hair growth for more than 30 years, and that Viviscal Limited is a subsidiary of Church & Dwight.[6] The supplement carries the usual dietary supplement disclaimer that its statements have not been evaluated by the FDA.[6]

paras: The core of every Viviscal product is a marine-derived collagen complex, which the company describes as the foundation of the range, supplemented with biotin, vitamin C and iron in most formulas, and zinc and copper in some.[6] Trial reports describe the supplement as a marine protein supplement designed to promote hair growth in people with temporary thinning hair associated with poor diet, stress, hormonal influences or abnormal menstrual cycles.[2] Reviews of nutraceuticals for androgenetic alopecia group it with other branded oral supplements such as Nutrafol, Nourkrin and Lambdapil.[5][7]

It is sold as a dietary supplement rather than a drug, so it is not approved by regulators for treating hair loss, and its labelling carries the standard statement that the FDA has not evaluated its claims.[6]

Viviscal is used by women with diffuse shedding or self-perceived thinning and by men with male pattern hair loss, either on its own or alongside other hair treatments. A journal review describes the 2015 clinical research programme, together with a panel discussion on thinning hair and current treatments, as the context in which these studies were conducted.[1] The 1992 study enrolled young men who had mostly previously used 2 percent topical minoxidil.[8]

A 1992 double-blind study in 40 young men with hereditary androgenic alopecia compared ViviScal with a fish extract for six months; it reported a mean 38 percent increase in non-vellus hair with ViviScal versus 2 percent with the control, and clinical and histological improvement in 19 of 20 treated subjects.[8] Most participants had previously used 2 percent topical minoxidil.[8]

A 90-day randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of Viviscal Extra Strength in adult women with self-perceived thinning hair (30 randomised to the supplement) reported a significant rise in terminal hair count versus placebo, less shedding, higher self-assessment and quality of life scores, and no adverse events.[2] A 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of Viviscal Man in men with male pattern hair loss reported significant increases in total and terminal hair density and lower hair-pull test results versus placebo; its authors note that male pattern baldness affects roughly half the adult population and can reduce quality of life.[3]

Registered studies cover women with self-perceived thinning hair: a 96-participant study that began in 2011, a 60-participant extra-strength study and a 40-participant professional-strength study that began in 2013.[9][10][11]

Reviews place these trials in a wider context. The 2023 JAMA Dermatology review searched through October 2021 and included 30 articles, 17 of them randomised trials, on nutritional interventions in people without known deficiency; it identified Viviscal among those with the highest-quality evidence of potential benefit, and the authors advised cautious interpretation.[4] A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of commercial oral supplements covered 14 studies with 967 participants, including Viviscal alongside Nutrafol, Nourkrin, Lambdapil and others, and reported significant improvements versus placebo including reduced telogen hair density.[5] A review of nutraceuticals for androgenetic alopecia and a network meta-analysis of hair regrowth treatments discuss the field more broadly.[7][12]

A 2023 review of marine-derived ingredients discusses their proposed effects on the hair cell cycle.[13] The company describes the marine collagen complex as supplying amino acids, and lists biotin as supporting follicle formation, zinc as supporting follicle cycling and copper as a building block in keratin.[6] Human mechanistic studies of Viviscal itself have not been published in the references above.

The trials above reported few or no adverse events, and the JAMA Dermatology review described supplement adverse effects as rare and mild.[2][4] The 2023 review of nutritional supplements stresses that safety and effectiveness of available products had been unclear before its compilation of the trials.[4]

Viviscal is a long-established name among hair supplements and appears in forum hair-loss discussions as a non-drug option that people suggest when others are wary of prescription treatments; one 2013 T Nation forum thread on hair loss mentions it that way.[14] It is positioned by its maker as a supplement for women and men, and the research programme behind it has been run largely in women with self-perceived thinning hair.[2][9][10][11]
